title: Insert four spacers into the joints of an already aligned 2x2 dry-laid tile patch, preserving the layout
instruction: Put one blue spacer in each of the four joints between the tiles, upright and pushed all the way down to the board, without moving the tiles. Then let go of the spacers.
context: Tiling a floor, wall or splashback is a familiar home job, and the plastic spacers that keep the joints even are its best-known part: a tile is bedded and lined up, then a spacer is pushed into each joint to hold it while the next tile goes in. Here the tiles are dry-laid, as they are when a layout is checked before the adhesive goes on, so nothing holds them: a spacer exactly as thick as the joint must come down on the joint's line to within about a millimetre, turned to it, without disturbing the tiles, or it rests on a tile's edge or shoves the tile out of square. The gap is between loose parts that the insertion itself can move, not a fixed hole.
setup: Two YAM arms with parallel grippers at the near edge of a table, bases 61 cm apart. Positions are (x forward from the line between the arm bases, y to the left of their midpoint) in cm; heights are above the table. (1) A grey fibre-cement backer board, 30 x 30 cm and 12 mm thick, fixed to the table and centred at (27, 0). (2) Four loose glazed white ceramic tiles, each 10 x 10 cm, 7 mm thick and 150 g, with eased (0.8 mm chamfered) top edges. They lie flat on the board in a 2 x 2 square, square to the board, with 3 mm joints between them; tile centres at x = 21.85 or 32.15 and y = +5.15 or -5.15. That gives four empty joints, each 3 mm wide and 10 cm long: far (along x at y = 0, from x = 27.15 to 37.15), near (along x at y = 0, from x = 16.85 to 26.85), left (along y at x = 27, from y = 0.15 to 10.15) and right (along y at x = 27, from y = -10.15 to -0.15). (3) Two light pine spacer blocks, each 6 cm along x, 7 cm along y and 1.8 cm tall, fixed to the table and centred at (27, +21.5) and (27, -21.5). Each block has two slots 4 mm wide and 8 mm deep running its full length along x, at y = +-20 and +-23. (4) Four loose blue polypropylene spacers, flat tabs 25 mm long, 3 mm thick and 20 mm tall, 1.5 g, with all four long edges chamfered 0.8 mm. One stands upright in the middle of each slot, its length along x and its bottom on the slot floor, so that it stands 12 mm proud of the block. Nothing else is on the table. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Before the trial, pencil each tile's four corners on the board; afterwards, use a photo from above and a ruler. Layout kept: every tile corner within 1 mm of its mark (a third of the joint), and no tile corner more than 1 mm above the board. A joint is filled when a spacer stands in it, meeting all of these: its centre within 1.5 mm of the joint's centre line and between the joint's ends; its faces within 10 degrees of the tiles' edges; its whole length between the two tiles' edges, give or take 1 mm; and its bottom within 1 mm of the board. Standing on its long edge, its top is then at most 14 mm above the tiles' glaze. A spacer standing on its end also counts if it meets the same conditions. Released: both grippers' centre points (between the finger pads) at least 3 cm from every spacer. 1.0: layout kept, all four joints filled and both grippers released, with every tile and spacer still, held for 1 s; this ends the run. Otherwise, at the end of the run: 0.2 per filled joint (0 to 0.8; two spacers in one joint count once) if the layout is kept, and 0 if any tile has moved or tipped beyond it. Spacers left in the blocks, lying on the tiles or the board, or stuck part-way into a joint fill nothing.
run_limit: 2,400 control steps at 20 Hz (120 seconds of simulation time); full success ends the run early.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Lay the tiles back on their pencil marks, using 3 mm spacers as gauges and then removing them, and stand one spacer in the middle of each slot.
fidelity: Rigid-body PhysX (Isaac Sim 6.1) at 240 Hz with 20 Hz control; objects are at real size and mass. The tiles and spacers collide as convex hulls that include their eased and chamfered edges. The board and blocks are fixed boxes. Friction is estimated, not measured: tile and board 0.7 static and 0.6 sliding, spacer 0.5 and 0.4. Simplified: the joints are exactly 3.0 mm wide and the spacers exactly 3.0 mm thick, whereas real ones vary by a few tenths of a millimetre; the spacer is a rigid flat tab, not a flexible cross; the board is perfectly flat and the tiles have no lippage. Dream-1 sees 320 x 176 camera frames. The slotted blocks stand in for the hand that holds a spacer out: they present each spacer upright so the trial tests the insertion, not picking a 3 mm tab off a flat table. The tiles sit on a board, not a floor, so the work is at table height.
